Price Discrimination

Watch the art of charging different prices for the same good. Switch between uniform pricing, third-degree, and first-degree discrimination.

Third-degree splits buyers into markets and matches marginal revenue to marginal cost in each. First-degree charges each buyer exactly their willingness to pay and turns all surplus into profit. Surprisingly, third-degree can destroy more welfare than one uniform price. Splitting markets is not always more efficient.

For example, say a stationery 🏪 shop sells ✏️ pencils. The owner charges a regular 🧑 friend 100 won but a first-time visitor 150. The friend buys happily at the low price, and the owner earns more overall. Each customer faces a different price tag.

In the same example, compute the deadweight loss under the uniform price and under third-degree discrimination, and discuss whether the folk claim that discrimination raises welfare always holds.

Show proof

  1. Uniform price: market 1 DWL is (6−2)(10−6)/2=8(6-2)(10-6)/2 = 8(6−2)(10−6)/2=8, market 2 is (6−2)(6−2)/2=8(6-2)(6-2)/2 = 8(6−2)(6−2)/2=8 — total 161616.

  2. Third-degree: market 1 gives (7−2)(10−5)/2=12.5(7-2)(10-5)/2 = 12.5(7−2)(10−5)/2=12.5, market 2 gives (5−2)(6−3)/2=4.5(5-2)(6-3)/2 = 4.5(5−2)(6−3)/2=4.5 — total 171717.

    Third-degree discrimination lowered welfare!

    Total output is 888 in both cases, but output is misallocated — shifted from high-marginal-value market 1 to low-marginal-value market 2.
